newsitem.title: USA: Pilot's lawyer hopeful judge will delay trial.
newsitem.headline: Pilot's lawyer hopeful judge will delay trial.

text.p: A lawyer for the female Air Force pilot scheduled to be court-martialed on charges of adultery said Monday he was optimistic that a judge would delay her trial while the Air Force considers her resignation bid.

"I am optimistic... that the judge will grant us some time," Frank Spinner, the civilian lawyer for Lt. Kelly Flinn, told a news conference shortly after he submitted her request for an honourable discharge to Minot Air Force Base officials.

Flinn, the Air Force's first female B-52 pilot, is seeking to resign with an honourable discharge to avoid court martial on adultery and other charges. The trial was scheduled to begin Tuesday at the base.

"The whole point of Lt. Flinn offering this resignation is to avoid a trial, to avoid the embarrassment that we believe it will bring on the Air Force as well as further embarrassment it will cause her," Spinner said.
But Spinner said he was seeking to delay the trial until June 2 also to gain more time to prepare for the court martial.

Flinn's lawyers submited the resignation request -- a thick, bound document that Spinner showed to reporters -- to the office of Col. Robert Elder, the 5th Bomb Wing Commander at Minot Air Force Base. Her lawyers confirmed that they had sent another copy via overnight mail to Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall in Washington.

Spinner said the document argued that an honourable discharge would not be an unreasonable outcome to Flinn's case. He said he had identified "numerous cases" in which Air Force members in similar circumstances had been allowed to remain on active duty.

"Our position is that it is not rare for someone who is charged with adultery even to remain on active duty or to receive an honourable discharge," Spinner said. "This is not precedent-setting if Lt. Flinn receives an honourable discharge."
Spinner acknowledged there was a possibility that the judge in the case, Col. Dennis Kansala, would deny the delay and that the trial would go forward Tuesday.

"One option would be to process the resignation request and (for) the trial to go forward. Even if there's a conviction, the secretary could still approve the request and that would eliminate the conviction," Spinner said.
The Air Force said in a statement that Col. Elder had received Flinn's request.

"Col. Elder will review the request and act on it in accordance with Air Force regulations," the statement said. "He has not had time to properly evaluate the request to ensure Lt. Flinn receives due process."
It was unclear how quickly the Air Force chain of command could process Flinn's request, but the decision on whether to grant the honourable discharge will likely fall to Widnall.
CNN quoted unnamed Pentagon sources on Monday saying that the Air Force had no intention of granting Flinn an honourable discharge since it would set an undesirable precedent.
Air Force Major Ron Lovas declined comment on the report, saying there would be no decision on Flinn's request until Tuesday. He said Widnall had not made a decision on the case.
"When appropriate, she'll review the facts in the case and make a decision," Lovas said, confirming that Widnall had received the discharge request from Flinn's attorneys.
Flinn has said she would rather go to trial than accept a less-than-honourable discharge, which Spinner said would preclude her from flying military planes for the National Guard.
Flinn, 26 and single, has acknowledged having had an affair with a married civilian and is also accused of having sex with a lower-ranking enlisted man. She is also accused of lying.

Conviction of adultery in a military trial is punishable by penalties ranging up to dishonourable discharge and possible fines and imprisonment. Critics have argued that Flinn's case highlights a double standard in the way the U.S. Armed Forces treats the issue of adultery among its male and female staff.
